newsitem.title: USA: YEAREND - Wheat bulls dethroned by Mother Nature.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Wheat bulls dethroned by Mother Nature.

text.p: It was a glorious battle, traders said -- the wheat market's joust with Mother Nature in 1996.

On the back of crop problems in Australia and elsewhere, and shrinking world stockpiles, wheat prices soared to record highs during the most volatile trading year that most hardened pit traders at the Chicago Board of Trade could remember.
Fears of damage to the U.S. crop -- a bellwether for world supplies -- came first from a winter drought and then a spring freeze in the U.S. Plains, the main U.S. wheat belt.
In Arizona, a rare fungus was detected, causing a quarantine of some areas and a temporary halt to U.S. exports.
Later, in Ohio and Indiana, torrential rains spawned more disease problems that rattled nerves of flour millers and bakers as well as worried traders.
But in the end the high yields and heavy plantings by U.S. wheat farmers produced a bumper crop and wheat prices eased back -- for now.
A ROLLERCOASTER MARKET
As tracked at the CBOT, wheat started 1996 at about $4.90 a bushel, up smartly from $4 a year earlier due to shrinking stockpiles in Europe and strong demand from Asia.
But that was only a springboard.
The market jumped to $7.50 in March -- nearly $2 above the prior world record price -- as panic buying set in at CBOT.
The price soon dropped back to $4.80, then rose again as high as $7.17 by early May against a rash of stories about crop diseases, winterkill damage, and plowed-under fields.
But the U.S. winter wheat harvest then began and a reality check set in. Despite crop losses, plantings had been huge.
As fears of damage from frost, insects and diseases eased, so did prices. By the end of May, wheat was quoted at $5.20.
As quality supplies continued to pour in, wheat kept falling. On Dec 30, CBOT March futures closed at $3.82.
"In the U.S. market, it was a decline in winter wheat production which this year got us over $7.00 in March," said Warren King, grain analyst for Cargill Investor Services.
"There had been doom, gloom and disaster in Kansas, Texas and Oklahoma but it just didn't turn out that way," King said. "There's been an almost 180 degree turn in 1996-97."
SUPPLIES LOOK SET TO RECOVER
Some wheat traders are convinced that with wheat crops again burgeoning in Europe, Canada, Australia and Argentina, the wheat market will be off the boil for most of 1997.
The U.S. Agriculture Department on December 13 estimated world wheat production for the 1996-97 crop year ending next July at 579.6 million tonnes, up 42.7 million tonnes from a year earlier.
The United States is expected to harvest 62.1 million tonnes, up from the 59.4 million a year earlier.

"This is a market you'll be telling your grandchildren about. The largest bull move in history followed by the largest bear market in history," said Charlie Sernatinger, the Chicago-based grain analyst for trading house E.D. and F. Man International.

"For next year the main feature will be early year price strength because of tight world and domestic ending stocks followed by a massive price break when the Northern Hemisphere crop comes in (in June and July)," Sernatinger said.
That scenario sounds surprisingly similar to a year ago, mainly because stocks of wheat remain historically low.
STOCKS, WEATHER TO BE WILD CARDS IN 1997?

In November the London-based International Grains Council estimated 1996/97 world wheat end-season stocks at 102 million tonnes, down from 104 million a month earlier. The 1995/96 end-stocks of 95 million tonnes were the lowest since 1979.
So while an expected rise in world wheat production is now the keynote for most wheat market bears who look for lower prices, there are experts quick to raise a caution flag.

"We've learned a lot this last year with regard to how tight the stocks in the U.S. and world can get before things start to happen," said Greg Doud, Research and Market Analyst for the U.S. Wheat Associates, an export promotion group.
Doud said the world wheat stocks-to-use ratio was now at 19.4 percent, against the 18.7 percent low last year -- the second tightest ratio since 1960, he added.
Doud also said location of wheat this year may play a more sensitive role than overall stocks or stocks-to-use data.
"A case in point was last week in Argentina. We got real excited real quick," Doud said.
Chicago wheat futures last week surged on fears that Argentina's crop was being hammered by heavy rains before a turn to drier weather eased market fears.
Argentina this winter is still expected to harvest a 15.5 million tonne wheat crop, up from 9.2 million last year.
DEMAND SIDE LOOKS LESS URGENT

Analysts say Russia, once the world's biggest grain buyer, will remain a minor player in the world wheat market because it lacks funds to buy. But Russia's wheat production this year is also expected to rise to 64.2 million tonnes, from 58.9 million.

Asia demand is always a wild card, mainly due to the unpredictability of crops in China. Right now it doesn't look like China will need to import much wheat with output pegged at 109.0 million tonnes, above last year's 102.2 million.
India, so far, has been the only surprise Asian buyer.

"In India the increasing population keeps raising the bar higher and higher with regard to wheat consumption," Doud said. "India's wheat consumption this year will be 64.6 million tonnes, last year it was 63.3 million and the year before that 57.7 million," he said.
On December 12, India said it would import two million tonnes of wheat this fiscal year to check rising prices, its first imports in four years.
Traders later said India bought one million tonnes from Australia and another 250,000 tonnes from Canada.
